claim: KLK3 (kallikrein-related peptidase 3) cleaves pro-VEGF-C, resulting in a mature protein that migrates at about 20 kDa in Western blotting analysis.
source: We could not demonstrate robust VEGF-C activation by KLK4 as predicted by Matsumura et al. (2005) (data not shown), but purified KLK3 cleaved pro-VEGF-C, resulting in a mature protein that migrated at about 20 kDa in Western blotting analysis (Figure 1A, lane 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text, demonstrating KLK3 cleavage of pro-VEGF-C.

claim: The monoclonal antibody 5C7 inhibits KLK3 protease activity when used in 2-fold molar excess.
source: To confirm that KLK3 was responsible for the cleavage, we inhibited its protease activity by using the monoclonal antibody 5C7 (Stenman et al., 1999) in 2-fold molar excess (Figure 1A, lane 1 versus lane 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using antibody 5C7 to inhibit KLK3 activity, with citation to Stenman et al., 1999.

claim: The majority of pro-VEGF-C is cleaved by KLK3 as shown by probing with antiserum 3/4.
source: Probing with antiserum 3/4, which recognizes both pro-VEGF-C and mature VEGF-C, showed that the majority of pro-VEGF-C had been cleaved by KLK3.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data using antiserum 3/4 to detect both forms of VEGF-C.

claim: KLK3-processed VEGF-C is biologically active in Ba/F3 cell assays.
source: We tested the KLK3-processed VEGF-C for its biological activity in Ba/F3 cells, which had been stably transfected with VEGFR/EpoR chimeras and found that it promoted the survival of both VEGFR-2/EpoR (Figure 1C) and VEGFR-3/EpoR cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Ba/F3 cell survival assays shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: KLK3 cleaves VEGF-C between Tyr-114 and Asn-115.
source: Edman degradation of the KLK3-processed VEGF-C revealed the amino-terminal sequence NTEIL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Thus, KLK3 cleaves VEGF-C between Tyr-114 and Asn-115, targeting a sequence similar to most of its cleavage sites in the seminogelins, which are the primary target proteins of KLK3 (Malm et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by Edman degradation data and comparison to known KLK3 cleavage sites in seminogelins, with citation to Malm et al., 2000.

claim: KLK3-cleaved VEGF-C is three N-terminal amino acid residues shorter than the mature VEGF-C generated by ADAMTS3.
source: The KLK3-cleaved VEGF-C is three N-terminal amino acid residues shorter than the mature VEGF-C generated by ADAMTS3 (Jeltsch et al., 2014) and 12 amino acid residues shorter than the mature VEGF-C produced by PC-3 cells (Figure 2) (Joukov et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison data shown in Figure 2 and citations to previous work on VEGF-C activation.

claim: Residues −7 to +1 relative to the KLK3 cleavage site and −4 to +4 relative to the ADAMTS3 cleavage site (KFAA↓AHY↓N) are 100% conserved among all mammals and birds analyzed.
source: We analyzed the VEGF-C amino acid sequences of 40 vertebrate species and found that residues −7 to +1 relative to the KLK3 cleavage site and −4 to +4 relative to the ADAMTS3 cleavage site (KFAA↓AHY↓N) are 100% conserved among all mammals and birds that were included in the analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative sequence analysis of VEGF-C orthologs from 40 vertebrate species.

claim: Significant differences in the VEGF-C cleavage site region were found in all fish species analyzed compared to mammals and birds.
source: However, we found significant differences in this area in all fish species analyzed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Human seminal plasma contains VEGF-C.
source: VEGF-C was detected in Western blots of sperm liquefied for approximately 20–30 min at room temperature by using antibody sc-374628 after VEGF-C precipitation with soluble forms of its receptors VEGFR-2 (VEGFR-2/Fc) and VEGFR-3 (VEGFR-3/Fc) or anti-VEGF-C antiserum 882 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot detection of VEGF-C in seminal plasma samples shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The affinity of seminal plasma VEGF-C towards VEGFR-2 is much weaker than towards VEGFR-3 in pull down assays.
source: The affinity of seminal plasma VEGF-C towards VEGFR-2 appeared to be much weaker than towards VEGFR-3 in the VEGF-C pull down assay (Figure 3A, compare lanes 4 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Seminal plasma VEGF-C is composed of inactive pro-VEGF-C and active mature VEGF-C.
source: The mobilities of the VEGF-C polypeptides indicated that it is composed of inactive pro-VEGF-C and active mature VEGF-C.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mobility patterns of VEGF-C polypeptides observed in Western blots.

claim: Seminal plasma stimulates VEGFR-3 phosphorylation in PAE cells stably expressing VEGFR-3.
source: Stimulation of VEGFR-3-transfected porcine aortic endothelial (PAE) cells with seminal plasma resulted in VEGFR-3 phosphorylation (Figure 3B, compare lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Seminal plasma stimulates VEGFR-2 phosphorylation in PAE cells stably expressing VEGFR-2 even more strongly than recombinant VEGF-C control.
source: VEGF-C stimulation of PAE cells stably expressing VEGFR-2 led to an even stronger phosphorylation than the recombinant VEGF-C control.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative phosphorylation assay data.

claim: Most of the VEGFR-2 phosphorylation by seminal plasma is blocked by soluble VEGFR-2/Fc but not by VEGFR-3/Fc.
source: Indeed, most of the VEGFR-2 phosphorylation was blocked when incubated with soluble VEGFR-2/Fc, but not by incubation with VEGFR-3/Fc (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by blocking experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: VEGF-D was not detected in seminal plasma.
source: In contrast, VEGF-D was not detected in seminal plasma (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative detection results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Fresh seminal fluid contains less processed VEGF-C than seminal fluid liquefied at 37°C.
source: When fresh ejaculates were immediately mixed with protease inhibitors, placed on ice and analyzed, less active VEGF-C was detected than in ejaculates that had been liquefied, indicating that pro-VEGF-C is converted into mature VEGF-C after ejaculation (Figure 3C), concurrently with sperm liquefaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of fresh versus liquefied seminal fluid shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pro-VEGF-C is converted into mature VEGF-C after ejaculation, concurrently with sperm liquefaction.
source: When fresh ejaculates were immediately mixed with protease inhibitors, placed on ice and analyzed, less active VEGF-C was detected than in ejaculates that had been liquefied, indicating that pro-VEGF-C is converted into mature VEGF-C after ejaculation (Figure 3C), concurrently with sperm liquefaction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that VEGF-C activation occurs during the liquefaction process.

claim: Ion chelation with CHELEX 100 or EDTA has no effect on VEGF-C activation in seminal plasma.
source: While the mature VEGF-C/pro-VEGF-C ratios of ion sequestered samples (50 mg/ml CHELEX 100 and 5 mM EDTA in lanes 2 and 4, respectively) were not different from the untreated sample (lane 6), lowering the pH tended to increase the activation of VEGF-C (lane 5), but the difference to untreated sample did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing ion chelation treatments to untreated samples.

claim: CCBE1 enhances KLK3-mediated cleavage of VEGF-C.
source: We found that KLK3-mediated cleavage of VEGF-C was enhanced by CCBE1 when CCBE1 or KLK3 amounts were titrated down so that only little VEGF-C processing occurred (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 demonstrating enhanced cleavage in the presence of CCBE1.

claim: Substantial amounts of CCBE1 are present in seminal plasma.
source: Substantial amounts of CCBE1 were detected in seminal plasma by Western blotting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), confirming published proteomics results (Jodar et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot detection data and confirmed by citation to proteomics studies.

claim: VEGF-C cleavage could be increased by CCBE1 in semen.
source: This indicates that VEGF-C cleavage could be increased by CCBE1 also in semen.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the presence of CCBE1 in seminal plasma and its ability to enhance KLK3-mediated VEGF-C cleavage.

claim: CCBE1 enhances the proteolytic activation of VEGF-C by ADAMTS3, but not by plasmin.
source: We have shown that CCBE1 enhances the proteolytic activation of VEGF-C by ADAMTS3, but not by plasmin (Jeltsch et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by Jeltsch et al., 2014.

claim: VEGF-CDMH (a form with partial removal of the N-terminal helix) binds to VEGFR-3 but only weakly or not at all to VEGFR-2 when produced in S2 cells.
source: Interestingly, unlike the corresponding VEGF-D form, this 'VEGF-CDMH' (for 'D Minor Homology') bound to VEGFR-3, but only weakly or not at all to VEGFR-2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by receptor binding assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: VEGF-CDMH produced in 293T cells does not bind to VEGFR-2 or VEGFR-3.
source: Because of this unexpected result, we performed the experiment using proteins produced in 293 T cells and found that in conditions where all other mature forms of VEGF-C interacted with their receptors as predicted, VEGF-CDMH did not bind to VEGFR-2 or VEGFR-3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by receptor binding assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The loss of binding of 293T-produced VEGF-CDMH is attributed to the extra N-terminal four amino acid residues of the mammalian linker.
source: Since the loss of binding compared to the S2 cell-produced VEGF-CDMH is not associated with a loss of receptor-interacting amino acid residues, we attributed the loss of binding to the extra N-terminal four amino acid residues of the mammalian linker (see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of binding properties and structural differences between S2 and 293T-produced proteins.

claim: Progressive shortening of the N-terminus of VEGF-C results in gradually decreased stimulation of VEGFR-2 and VEGFR-3 phosphorylation.
source: The receptor phosphorylation results mirrored the binding results. The longest mature VEGF-C resulted in the strongest stimulation, and progressive shortening of the N-terminus resulted in gradually decreased stimulation of the receptor phosphorylation (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by receptor phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: VEGF-CDMH purified from S2 cells stimulates phosphorylation of VEGFR-3 but not or only very weakly of VEGFR-2.
source: We also tested the activity of purified VEGF-CDMH expressed in S2 cells. In agreement with the binding results, 100 ng/ml VEGF-CDMH did stimulate the phosphorylation of VEGFR-3 but not or only very weakly of VEGFR-2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by receptor phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The DMH-form of mature VEGF-C can be produced by proteolytic processing of a longer mature form of VEGF-C by an unknown protease.
source: N-terminal sequencing of the form produced from the longer cDNA revealed that about ⅔ had the KSIDNE… N-terminus, and about ⅓ had AAAHYN... as N-terminus. Hence, the DMH-form of mature VEGF-C can also be produced by proteolytic processing of a longer mature form of VEGF-C by a yet unknown protease.
evidence: The claim is supported by N-terminal sequencing data showing secondary processing of VEGF-C.

claim: Cathepsin D was identified as the most likely candidate protease for VEGF-C activation in human saliva through mass spectrometric analysis.
source: We enriched the VEGF-C activating component of human saliva by cation exchange chromatography (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and subjected the fractions containing the peak activity to mass spectrometric analysis. Among the highest scoring proteases (Supplementary file 2), cathepsin D was identified as the most likely candidate due to the cleavage context of the DMH-form of VEGF-C (Leu-118↓Lys-119).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cleavage site analysis.

claim: Cathepsin D cleaves pro-VEGF-C into active VEGF-C.
source: Using purified recombinant proteins, we confirmed that cathepsin D cleaves pro-VEGF-C into active VEGF-C (Figure 6A and Figure 7AB) and performs a secondary activation of the minor, mature form of VEGF-C (Figure 6A and Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using purified recombinant proteins shown in Figures 6A and 7AB.

claim: Cathepsin D performs a secondary activation of the minor, mature form of VEGF-C.
source: Using purified recombinant proteins, we confirmed that cathepsin D cleaves pro-VEGF-C into active VEGF-C (Figure 6A and Figure 7AB) and performs a secondary activation of the minor, mature form of VEGF-C (Figure 6A and Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and 7F.

claim: Cathepsin D activates pro-VEGF-D.
source: Because the sequence contexts of the cleavage sites of cathepsin D and KLK3 are conserved between VEGF-C and VEGF-D (see Figure 2), we investigated, if also cathepsin D and KLK3 could activate pro-VEGF-D. Indeed, cathepsin D activated pro-VEGF-D and performed a secondary activation of the longer, mature form of VEGF-D.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cathepsin D performs a secondary activation of the longer, mature form of VEGF-D.
source: Indeed, cathepsin D activated pro-VEGF-D and performed a secondary activation of the longer, mature form of VEGF-D. The cleavage of mature VEGF-D was rapid and complete (Figure 6C), whereas the cleavage of both pro-VEGF-C and mature VEGF-C was slower and incomplete even after 16 hr (Figure 6AB).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The cleavage of mature VEGF-D by cathepsin D is rapid and complete.
source: The cleavage of mature VEGF-D was rapid and complete (Figure 6C), whereas the cleavage of both pro-VEGF-C and mature VEGF-C was slower and incomplete even after 16 hr (Figure 6AB).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course cleavage data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The cleavage of both pro-VEGF-C and mature VEGF-C by cathepsin D is slower and incomplete even after 16 hours.
source: The cleavage of mature VEGF-D was rapid and complete (Figure 6C), whereas the cleavage of both pro-VEGF-C and mature VEGF-C was slower and incomplete even after 16 hr (Figure 6AB).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course cleavage data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: Cathepsin D processing of mature VEGF-D abolishes most of its activity in the Ba/F3-VEGFR-3/EpoR assay.
source: As expected, the cathepsin D processing of mature VEGF-D abolished most of its activity in the Ba/F3-VEGFR-3/EpoR assay (Figure 7C) and reduced, but did not abolish its activity in the Ba/F3-VEGFR-2/EpoR assay (Figure 7D), while processing of pro-VEGF-D stimulated the phosphorylation of VEGFR-2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ba/F3 cell assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Cathepsin D processing of mature VEGF-D reduces, but does not abolish its activity in the Ba/F3-VEGFR-2/EpoR assay.
source: As expected, the cathepsin D processing of mature VEGF-D abolished most of its activity in the Ba/F3-VEGFR-3/EpoR assay (Figure 7C) and reduced, but did not abolish its activity in the Ba/F3-VEGFR-2/EpoR assay (Figure 7D), while processing of pro-VEGF-D stimulated the phosphorylation of VEGFR-2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ba/F3 cell assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cathepsin D processing of pro-VEGF-D stimulates the phosphorylation of VEGFR-2.
source: As expected, the cathepsin D processing of mature VEGF-D abolished most of its activity in the Ba/F3-VEGFR-3/EpoR assay (Figure 7C) and reduced, but did not abolish its activity in the Ba/F3-VEGFR-2/EpoR assay (Figure 7D), while processing of pro-VEGF-D stimulated the phosphorylation of VEGFR-2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by phosphorylation assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: KLK3 activates pro-VEGF-D.
source: KLK3 also activated pro-VEGF-D (Figure 6D and Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D and 7E.

claim: KLK3 has two additional cleavage sites in pro-VEGF-D beyond the previously reported site.
source: When VEGF-D was produced from a full-length cDNA using the baculovirus system, a significant fraction of the protein did not undergo processing by proprotein convertases. This allowed us to observe two additional KLK3 cleavage sites in pro-VEGF-D. One of these cleavages has been reported previously (Stacker et al., 1999a); the other cleavage mimics the C-terminal cleavage catalyzed by proprotein convertases that cleave between the VHD and the N-terminal propeptide (Figure 6D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D and 7—figure supplement 2, with one cleavage site cited to Stacker et al., 1999a.

claim: Both the KLK3-form and the cathepsin D-form of VEGF-C stimulate lymphangiogenesis and angiogenesis in mouse skeletal muscle.
source: To confirm that the two new forms of VEGF-C have also an effect in-vivo, we transduced mouse skeletal muscle (tibialis anterior) with recombinant adeno-associated viruses serotype 9 encoding the KLK3- or the cathepsin D- (CATD) form of VEGF-C. Both vectors stimulated lymphangiogenesis and angiogenesis (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The response to the KLK3-form of VEGF-C is stronger compared to the cathepsin D-form in mouse skeletal muscle.
source: As expected on the basis of the binding and receptor phosphorylation results, the response to the KLK3-form was stronger compared to the cathepsin D-form.
evidence: The claim is inferred from in vivo experimental results and is consistent with in vitro binding and phosphorylation data.

claim: Both the KLK3-form and cathepsin D-form of VEGF-C appear to give a stronger response compared to the ADAMTS3-form, but the higher expression level of the shorter VEGF-C forms likely explains most of this difference.
source: Both forms appeared to give a stronger response compared to the positive control (the ADAMTS3-form of VEGF-C), but the higher expression level of the shorter VEGF-C forms likely explains most of this difference (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo data and expression level measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: VEGF-A is essential for early embryonic development and for successful implantation of the embryo into the uterus.
source: Vascular endothelial growth factor VEGF-A is essential for early embryonic development and for successful implantation of the embryo into the uterus (Binder et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Binder et al., 2014.

claim: VEGF-A acts on both vascular and non-vascular targets during implantation.
source: VEGF-A acts in this function on both vascular and non-vascular targets (Hannan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hannan et al., 2011.

claim: The primary function of VEGF-C is stimulation of growth of the lymphatic vasculature.
source: The primary function of the closely related growth factor VEGF-C is stimulation of growth of the lymphatic vasculature (Rauniyar et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rauniyar et al., 2018.

claim: VEGF-C is required for ovarian follicle growth and maturation and endometrial lymphangiogenesis.
source: VEGF-C is required for ovarian follicle growth and maturation and endometrial lymphangiogenesis (Rogers, 2008; Rutkowski et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rogers, 2008 and Rutkowski et al., 2013.

claim: VEGF-A is secreted as an active growth factor.
source: Unlike VEGF-A, which is secreted as an active growth factor (Leung et al., 1989), VEGF-C is secreted as an inactive precursor (pro-VEGF-C), which requires two proteolytic cleavages for activation (Jeltsch et al., 2014; Joukov et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Leung et al., 1989.

claim: VEGF-C is secreted as an inactive precursor (pro-VEGF-C), which requires two proteolytic cleavages for activation.
source: Unlike VEGF-A, which is secreted as an active growth factor (Leung et al., 1989), VEGF-C is secreted as an inactive precursor (pro-VEGF-C), which requires two proteolytic cleavages for activation (Jeltsch et al., 2014; Joukov et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jeltsch et al., 2014 and Joukov et al., 1997.

claim: The first C-terminal cleavage resulting in pro-VEGF-C occurs constitutively in the endoplasmic reticulum and is mediated by proprotein convertases.
source: The first C-terminal cleavage resulting in pro-VEGF-C occurs constitutively in the endoplasmic reticulum and is mediated by proprotein convertases (Siegfried et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Siegfried et al., 2003.

claim: The second cleavage of VEGF-C takes place in the extracellular environment, is highly regulated and requires the assembly of a trimeric complex consisting of VEGF-C, the ADAMTS3 metalloproteinase and the 'cofactor' CCBE1.
source: The second cleavage takes place in the extracellular environment, is highly regulated and requires the assembly of a trimeric complex consisting of VEGF-C, the ADAMTS3 metalloproteinase and the 'cofactor' CCBE1 (Bui et al., 2016; Jeltsch et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bui et al., 2016 and Jeltsch et al., 2014.

claim: Alternative activation of VEGF-C by plasmin has been shown in vitro, but its significance under physiological settings is unknown.
source: Alternative activation by plasmin has been shown in vitro, but its significance under physiological settings is unknown (McColl et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McColl et al., 2003 and acknowledges uncertainty about physiological relevance.

claim: VEGF-D is the closest paralog of VEGF-C.
source: VEGF-D is the closest paralog of VEGF-C (Achen et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Achen et al., 1998.

claim: VEGF-D is lymphangiogenic.
source: Similar to VEGF-C, it is lymphangiogenic (Veikkola et al., 2001), but appears to have a higher angiogenic potential than VEGF-C (Byzova et al., 2002; Rissanen et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Veikkola et al., 2001.

claim: VEGF-D appears to have a higher angiogenic potential than VEGF-C.
source: Similar to VEGF-C, it is lymphangiogenic (Veikkola et al., 2001), but appears to have a higher angiogenic potential than VEGF-C (Byzova et al., 2002; Rissanen et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Byzova et al., 2002 and Rissanen et al., 2003.

claim: The proteolytic activation of VEGF-D is very similar to that of VEGF-C.
source: The proteolytic activation of VEGF-D is very similar to that of VEGF-C (Stacker et al., 1999a), but it deploys distinct, so far unknown proteases (Bui et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stacker et al., 1999a.

claim: VEGF-D deploys distinct, so far unknown proteases for its activation.
source: The proteolytic activation of VEGF-D is very similar to that of VEGF-C (Stacker et al., 1999a), but it deploys distinct, so far unknown proteases (Bui et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bui et al., 2016.

claim: Many kallikrein-related peptidases are highly expressed in the prostate.
source: Many kallikrein-related peptidases are highly expressed in the prostate, and some prostate-derived cell lines, such as the immortalized human normal prostate epithelial (NPrEC) or PC-3 cells — from which VEGF-C was originally cloned — express high amounts of VEGF-C (Grennan, 2006; Joukov et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by general knowledge about kallikrein expression patterns.

claim: Some prostate-derived cell lines, such as NPrEC or PC-3 cells, express high amounts of VEGF-C.
source: Many kallikrein-related peptidases are highly expressed in the prostate, and some prostate-derived cell lines, such as the immortalized human normal prostate epithelial (NPrEC) or PC-3 cells — from which VEGF-C was originally cloned — express high amounts of VEGF-C (Grennan, 2006; Joukov et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grennan, 2006 and Joukov et al., 1996.

claim: VEGF-C was originally cloned from PC-3 cells.
source: Many kallikrein-related peptidases are highly expressed in the prostate, and some prostate-derived cell lines, such as the immortalized human normal prostate epithelial (NPrEC) or PC-3 cells — from which VEGF-C was originally cloned — express high amounts of VEGF-C (Grennan, 2006; Joukov et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Joukov et al., 1996.

claim: Matsumura et al. (2005) identified VEGF-C as a potential substrate for KLK4 in a peptide library scan.
source: In a peptide library scan, Matsumura et al. (2005) identified VEGF-C as a potential substrate for KLK4.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Matsumura et al., 2005.

claim: KLK3 is the major protease in human semen.
source: In this study, we show that KLK3, the major protease in human semen, is able to specifically activate VEGF-C and VEGF-D.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about seminal plasma composition.

claim: KLK3 is able to specifically activate VEGF-C and VEGF-D.
source: In this study, we show that KLK3, the major protease in human semen, is able to specifically activate VEGF-C and VEGF-D.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cathepsin D cleavage of VEGF-C results in a novel, predominantly VEGFR-3-binding form of VEGF-C.
source: We further show that cathepsin D cleavage of VEGF-C results in a novel, predominantly VEGFR-3-binding form of VEGF-C, and that cathepsin D cleavage of VEGF-D at the homologous site results in a VEGFR-2-specific (minor mature) form of VEGF-D.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on receptor binding and phosphorylation presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cathepsin D cleavage of VEGF-D at the homologous site results in a VEGFR-2-specific (minor mature) form of VEGF-D.
source: We further show that cathepsin D cleavage of VEGF-C results in a novel, predominantly VEGFR-3-binding form of VEGF-C, and that cathepsin D cleavage of VEGF-D at the homologous site results in a VEGFR-2-specific (minor mature) form of VEGF-D.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on receptor binding and activity presented in the manuscript.

claim: KLK3/PSA is widely known as a prostate cancer marker.
source: Kallikrein-related peptidase 3 (KLK3) or prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is widely known as a prostate cancer marker (Lilja et al., 2008), which may also participate in prostate cancer development (Koistinen and Stenman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lilja et al., 2008 and represents established medical knowledge.

claim: KLK3/PSA may participate in prostate cancer development.
source: Kallikrein-related peptidase 3 (KLK3) or prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is widely known as a prostate cancer marker (Lilja et al., 2008), which may also participate in prostate cancer development (Koistinen and Stenman, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Koistinen and Stenman, 2012 and is presented as speculative.

claim: PSA/KLK3 is the major protease responsible for seminal clot liquefaction.
source: PSA/KLK3 is also the major protease responsible for seminal clot liquefaction, and thus plays a role in reproduction.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about KLK3 function in semen.

claim: The angiogenic effect of VEGF-A is required for implantation.
source: The angiogenic effect of VEGF-A is required for example for implantation (Torry et al., 2007) and corpus luteum formation (Reynolds et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Torry et al., 2007.

claim: The angiogenic effect of VEGF-A is required for corpus luteum formation.
source: The angiogenic effect of VEGF-A is required for example for implantation (Torry et al., 2007) and corpus luteum formation (Reynolds et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reynolds et al., 2000.

claim: VEGF-A levels in human seminal plasma are variable, typically between 10–20 ng/ml.
source: VEGF-A levels in human seminal plasma are variable, typically between 10–20 ng/ml (Brown et al., 1995; Obermair et al., 1999), and VEGF-A has been implicated as a fertility factor that acts on sperm cells (Obermair et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1995 and Obermair et al., 1999.

claim: VEGF-A has been implicated as a fertility factor that acts on sperm cells.
source: VEGF-A levels in human seminal plasma are variable, typically between 10–20 ng/ml (Brown et al., 1995; Obermair et al., 1999), and VEGF-A has been implicated as a fertility factor that acts on sperm cells (Obermair et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Obermair et al., 1999.

claim: Sperm motility has been reported to increase slightly as a response to VEGF-A.
source: Sperm motility has been reported to increase slightly as a response to VEGF-A (Iyibozkurt et al., 2009), and overexpression of a testis-specific VEGF-A transgene resulted in infertility (Korpelainen et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iyibozkurt et al., 2009.

claim: Overexpression of a testis-specific VEGF-A transgene resulted in infertility.
source: Sperm motility has been reported to increase slightly as a response to VEGF-A (Iyibozkurt et al., 2009), and overexpression of a testis-specific VEGF-A transgene resulted in infertility (Korpelainen et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Korpelainen et al., 1998.

claim: Lymphangiogenesis is required for ovarian follicle maturation.
source: VEGF-C is the lymphangiogenic counterpart of VEGF-A, and lymphangiogenesis is required for ovarian follicle maturation (Rutkowski et al., 2013), corpus luteum formation (Abe et al., 2014; Nitta et al., 2011) and uterine implantation (Red-Horse, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rutkowski et al., 2013.

claim: Lymphangiogenesis is required for corpus luteum formation.
source: VEGF-C is the lymphangiogenic counterpart of VEGF-A, and lymphangiogenesis is required for ovarian follicle maturation (Rutkowski et al., 2013), corpus luteum formation (Abe et al., 2014; Nitta et al., 2011) and uterine implantation (Red-Horse, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abe et al., 2014 and Nitta et al., 2011.

claim: Lymphangiogenesis is required for uterine implantation.
source: VEGF-C is the lymphangiogenic counterpart of VEGF-A, and lymphangiogenesis is required for ovarian follicle maturation (Rutkowski et al., 2013), corpus luteum formation (Abe et al., 2014; Nitta et al., 2011) and uterine implantation (Red-Horse, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Red-Horse, 2008.

claim: VEGF-C and VEGF-D are hormonally regulated in the reproductive system.
